title: Cap. IV Arg. 2: Heb. 11:6 — without that by which one cannot please God, none can be elected
latin: Arg. 2. Secundo argumentantur ex verbis Apostoli, Hebr. xi. 6. Sine fide impossibile est placere Deo. Unde tale argumentum exstruunt; Sine quo impossibile est placere Deo, sine eo impossibile est a Deo quenquam eligi ad salutem: Sine fide impossibile est placere Deo: Ergo. Majorem certam esse pronunciant, quandoquidem eligere ad salutem, summa est dilectio quam homini Deus praestare potest, sive maxima ipsius in homine dilectio.
pass_a: Argument 2. Second they argue from the words of the Apostle, Heb. 11:6. Without faith it is impossible to please God. Whence they construct such an argument; Without that without which it is impossible to please God, without it it is impossible that anyone be elected by God to salvation: Without faith it is impossible to please God: Therefore. They pronounce the Major certain, inasmuch as to elect to salvation is the highest love which God can show to a man, or his greatest love in a man.
pass_b: Arg. 2. Second they argue from Heb. 11:6 — Without faith it is impossible to please God — and build this: Without that without which one cannot please God, no one can be elected by God to salvation; without faith one cannot please God; therefore. They call the Major certain, since electing to salvation is the highest love God can show a man — his greatest love toward a man.

lemmas.lemma: Sine fide impossibile est placere Deo
lemmas.gloss: without faith impossible to please God

title: Cap. IV Arg. 2 Sol: Apostle twisted — faith here actual, not foreseen; Enoch walked with God
latin: Sol. Ad ipsa verba Apostoli primo respondemus, Ea pessime, et in sensum ab instituto Apostolico prorsus alienum, torqueri. Nam fides hoc in loco non praevisam fidem hominis nondum existentis, sed actualem, atque jam vires suas exercentem demonstrat. Hoc perspicuum est ex illo altero verbo εὐηρέστησεν, Placere, quod Apostolus ex Septuaginta Interpretum versione mutuatus est. Sic enim illi Genes. v. 24. εὐηρέστησεν Ἐνὼχ τῷ Θεῷ. At in Hebraeo habetur, continue ambulavit cum Deo: id est, Non est imitatus ejus saeculi nequitiam, sed corde sincero jugiter Deo servivit, Deumque caste coluit. Nihil igitur aliud dicere voluit Apostolus, quam neminem posse absque fide vitam piam Deoque placentem ducere; quod exemplo Enochi voluit confirmare. Miro igitur ingenio sunt Remonstrantes, qui potuerunt electionem suam ex fidei praevisione pendulam hinc exsculpere.
pass_a: Solution. To the Apostle's words themselves we first answer, That they are twisted most badly, and into a sense wholly alien from the Apostolic purpose. For faith in this place shows not the foreseen faith of a man not yet existing, but actual faith, and already exercising its powers. This is clear from that other word εὐηρέστησεν, To please, which the Apostle borrowed from the version of the Seventy Interpreters. For so they at Gen. 5:24, Enoch pleased God. But in the Hebrew it is had, he walked continually with God: that is, He did not imitate the wickedness of his age, but with a sincere heart continually served God, and purely worshiped God. The Apostle therefore willed to say nothing else than that no one can lead a pious life pleasing to God without faith; which he willed to confirm by the example of Enoch. Of wondrous genius therefore are the Remonstrants, who were able to carve out from here their election hanging from foresight of faith.
pass_b: Sol. First to the Apostle's words: they are twisted badly into a sense wholly alien to his purpose. Faith here is not the foreseen faith of a man not yet existing, but actual faith already at work. That is clear from εὐηρέστησεν, to please — which Paul takes from the LXX at Gen. 5:24, Enoch pleased God; the Hebrew is he walked continually with God — he did not imitate his age's wickedness but served God sincerely and worshiped him purely. So the Apostle means only that no one can lead a pious life pleasing to God without faith, confirmed by Enoch's example. Wondrous ingenuity in the Remonstrants, who carved from this their election hanging on foresight of faith.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 2 Sol: Major stuffed with equivocations — sine quo as condition vs means; elect infants
latin: Sed ipsum syllogismum ventilemus. Major propositio, Sine quo impossibile est placere Deo, sine eo impossibile est eligi quenquam ad salutem, tota farcta est aequivocationibus. Vocabula illa, sine quo, intelligi possunt dupliciter: sine quo praeviso et praeconsiderato ut antecedanea conditione nemo potest eligi ad salutem a Deo; vel, sine quo tanquam medio praeparato et destinato impossibile est eligi quenquam ad salutem. Priore sensu causam attingit, sed manifeste falsa est: Posteriore ne attingit quidem, et tamen non est absolutae veritatis. Nam quidem eatenus Deo placent, ut ad vitam aeternam eligantur, in quibus Deus non praevidet fidem omnino, nedum antecedaneam. Exemplo sint electi illi infantes qui moriuntur, priusquam per aetatem credere, aut in fide perseverare possint. Quod enim nunquam futurum est, a Deo non praevidetur: cum objectum praescientiae sit quiddam infallibiliter futurum.
pass_a: But let us ventilate the syllogism itself. The Major proposition, Without that without which it is impossible to please God, without it it is impossible that anyone be elected to salvation, is wholly stuffed with equivocations. Those words, without which, can be understood doubly: without which, foreseen and preconsidered as an antecedent condition, no one can be elected to salvation by God; or, without which as a prepared and destined means it is impossible that anyone be elected to salvation. In the prior sense it touches the cause, but is manifestly false: In the latter it does not even touch it, and yet is not of absolute truth. For indeed they so far please God that they are elected to eternal life, in whom God does not foresee faith at all, much less antecedent faith. Let those elect infants be an example who die before by age they can believe, or persevere in faith. For what will never be future is not foreseen by God: since the object of foresight is something infallibly future.
pass_b: Now the syllogism. The Major — Without that without which one cannot please God, no one can be elected to salvation — is stuffed with equivocations. Without which can mean: without which, foreseen as an antecedent condition, no one can be elected; or without which as a prepared, destined means no one can be elected. The first sense touches the cause but is manifestly false; the second does not even touch it, and still is not absolute truth. Some please God unto election to eternal life in whom God foresees no faith at all, still less antecedent faith — for example elect infants who die before they can believe or persevere. What will never be is not foreseen; foresight's object is something infallibly future.

lemmas.gloss: elect infants who die before faith

title: Cap. IV Arg. 2 Sol: placere Deo = walk with God — without actual faith election would be temporal
latin: Dein, verba illa, placere Deo, non uno modo accipi possunt. Sensu Paulino nihil aliud indicant, quam facere opera Deo placentia, vel (ut ex originali textu notavimus) ambulare cum Deo. Jam attendite quam absonum sit, neminem potuisse unquam a Deo eligi, nisi prius ea omnia habeat sine quibus opera nostra Deo placere non possunt. Profecto absque fide actuali, addo etiam, et charitate, nemo potest hoc modo placere Deo, (aut quod Enochus fecit) cum Deo ambulare. Si ulla vis inesset huic argumento, electio omnis esset temporalis, et justificationem ac sanctificationem sequeretur.
pass_a: Further, those words, to please God, cannot be taken in one manner only. In the Pauline sense they indicate nothing else than to do works pleasing to God, or (as we noted from the original text) to walk with God. Now attend how dissonant it is, that no one could ever have been elected by God, unless he first have all those things without which our works cannot please God. Certainly without actual faith, I add also, and charity, no one can in this manner please God, (or what Enoch did) walk with God. If any force were in this argument, all election would be temporal, and would follow justification and sanctification.
pass_b: Further, to please God is not one sense only. Paulinely it means doing works pleasing to God, or (from the original) walking with God. Mark how absurd it is that no one could ever be elected unless he first has all that our works need to please God. Without actual faith — and charity too — no one can please God that way, or walk with God as Enoch did. If this argument had force, all election would be temporal and would follow justification and sanctification.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 2 Sol: two pleasing — destined vs adopted; Orange 25; first love from God's fountain
latin: Porro recte dicimus quosdam placere Deo prae aliis, ut destinatos ad fidem et vitam aeternam; quosdam etiam placere Deo ut Dei filios actu jam adoptatos, sanctificatos, et ad jus vitae aeternae acceptatos. Priore sensu (quem nos respicere debemus in hac controversia) non modo possibile est ut quis ante habitam vel praevisam suam fidem placeat Deo, sed plane impossibile est ut aliter placeat. Optime Concilium Arausicanum, canone 25. Displicentes amati sumus, ut fieret in nobis unde placeremus. Si enim nullum beneficium a Deo accipere possemus, nisi prius ei placeremus, placere autem non possemus, nisi prius fidem habeamus: aut ipsum fidei beneficium a nobis, non a Deo habemus, aut dabitur processus in infinitum. Scire igitur oportet, rationem primæ complacentiae, sive amoris Divini erga lapsam creaturam, non in hominis bona aliqua qualitate antecedanea esse quaerendam, sed ex ipso fonte Divini amoris esse arcessendam. Nam amor est primum donum, in quo caetera omnia donantur: et amor Dei hoc habet singulare, quod non invenit sed facit suum objectum sibi amabile. Deut. vii. 7, 8. Te elegit Dominus Deus tuus, ut sis ei populus peculiaris, quia dilexit vos Dominus, non quia cunctas gentes numero vinceretis.
pass_a: Further we rightly say that certain ones please God before others, as destined to faith and eternal life; certain ones also please God as sons of God already actually adopted, sanctified, and accepted to the right of eternal life. In the prior sense (which we ought to regard in this controversy) it is not only possible that someone please God before his faith had or foreseen, but plainly impossible that he please otherwise. Most well the Council of Orange, canon 25. Displeasing we were loved, that there might be made in us whence we might please. For if we could receive no benefit from God, unless we first pleased him, but we could not please, unless we first have faith: either we have the benefit of faith itself from ourselves, not from God, or a process into infinity will be given. One ought therefore to know that the reason of the first complacency, or of the Divine love toward the fallen creature, is not to be sought in some antecedent good quality of man, but is to be fetched from the very fountain of Divine love. For love is the first gift, in which all the rest are gifted: and the love of God has this singular, that it does not find but makes its object lovable to itself. Deut. 7:7, 8. The Lord your God chose you, that you might be to him a peculiar people, because the Lord loved you, not because you would surpass all nations in number.
pass_b: Further: some please God before others as destined to faith and eternal life; some please as sons already adopted, sanctified, and accepted to the right of eternal life. In the prior sense (ours in this controversy) it is not only possible that one please God before faith had or foreseen — it is plainly impossible to please otherwise. Best Orange canon 25: Displeasing we were loved, that there might be made in us whence we might please. If we could receive no gift from God unless we first pleased him, and could not please without faith first, then either faith's gift is from us not God, or you get an infinite regress. So the reason of first complacency — divine love toward the fallen creature — is not some antecedent good quality in man, but must be fetched from the fountain of divine love. Love is the first gift in which all others are given; and God's love has this singular: it does not find but makes its object lovable to itself (Deut. 7:7–8).

title: Cap. IV Arg. 2 Sol close: election from amor benevolentiae not amicitiae — Remonstrants elide their own nerve
latin: Denique, quod ad confirmationem Majoris afferebatur, Eligere ad salutem esse effectum summae dilectionis, ac proinde neminem posse eligi a Deo, nisi qui per fidem saltem praevisam sit ei gratus et acceptus, hoc, inquam, facile refellitur et enervatur. Nam electio est effectus amoris, sed non illius amoris amicitiae de quo intelligenda sunt illa verba, Enoch placuit Deo; sed illius amoris, quem Schola appellat amorem sive benevolentiae. Effecta prioris amoris tendunt in solos fideles et pios, sed effecta posterioris in impios et incredulos, ut illis inspiret fidem et sanctitatem, imo in nondum natos, ut illis destinet vitam aeternam. Esse quendam Dei amorem qui exseritur erga impios ante fidem et conversionem ne diffiteri quidem possunt Remonstrantes; et tamen fatendo, hujus argumenti nervos elidunt. Videte quae de Antecedente et consequente amore scribunt, Colloq. Hag. pag. 183, Edit. Bertii.
pass_a: Finally, what was brought for confirmation of the Major, That to elect to salvation is an effect of the highest love, and therefore no one can be elected by God, unless he who through faith at least foreseen is pleasing and acceptable to him, this, I say, is easily refuted and enervated. For election is an effect of love, but not of that love of friendship of which those words are to be understood, Enoch pleased God; but of that love which the School calls love or of benevolence. The effects of the prior love tend unto the faithful and pious alone, but the effects of the latter unto the impious and unbelieving, that it may inspire faith and holiness in them, nay unto those not yet born, that it may destine eternal life to them. That there is a certain love of God which is put forth toward the impious before faith and conversion the Remonstrants cannot even deny; and yet by confessing, they strike out the nerves of this argument. See what they write concerning Antecedent and consequent love, Hague Colloquy p. 183, Bertius's edition.
pass_b: Finally, their Major's confirmation — electing to salvation is an effect of highest love, so no one can be elected unless through faith at least foreseen he is pleasing and acceptable — is easily refuted. Election is an effect of love, but not of that friendship-love of Enoch pleased God; rather of the love the School calls benevolence. Effects of friendship-love tend only to the faithful and pious; effects of benevolence tend to the impious and unbelieving, to inspire faith and holiness in them — even to the not-yet-born, to destine them eternal life. The Remonstrants cannot even deny a love of God put forth toward the impious before faith and conversion; and by confessing it they cut the nerves of this argument. See what they write on antecedent and consequent love, Hague Colloquy p. 183 (Bertius).
